You are here Step 9 of 9, Maintain · 9.1 Maintain Eligibility

Use ChatGPT to Plan Beyond a Medicaid Approval Before You Need One

Four prompts to write down what you’ve heard about life after approval, find where the family’s records are, name the changes that may be coming, and set a simple review routine.

Download PDF

Where you are

Dad doesn’t need Medicaid today, and he may never. But you’ve heard that approval isn’t the end of the process, and if the day came you couldn’t say where his records are or who would handle the letters.

This guide gives you four ChatGPT prompts to organize what you already know and to see what you don't know yet. It is preparation, not an assessment. Use only information you have permission to share, with names, ID numbers, case numbers, and account numbers removed. The AI organizes and drafts; it does not know your state’s Medicaid rules, and it does not decide what has to be reported or whether anything affects eligibility. Bring those questions to the Medicaid agency, your Medicaid planner, or an elder law attorney. The agency’s own notices are the authority on dates and requirements.

What you'll have at the end

You know where the important records are kept, who would handle Medicaid matters, which changes the family would ask a professional about first, and when you’ll look at it all again.

A one-page list: Where our records are, Who would handle what, Changes we’d ask about first, and When we’ll review.

Before you start

  • A rough idea of where Dad keeps statements, legal papers, and insurance and care records.
  • The names of the family members who help with his paperwork.
  • Anything you expect to change in the next few years: a move, a sale, an inheritance. A guess is fine.
Prompt 1

Write down what you’ve heard about life after approval

Why this matters

Most families’ picture of Medicaid stops at the word “approved.” Sorting what you were told from what you’re assuming shows you what to ask, long before it matters.

What you'll need

A few lines on what you’ve heard or read about what happens after someone is approved, and who told you.

Copy this prompt

My father is not on Medicaid and may never need it. I’m planning ahead. Here is what I’ve heard or read about what happens after someone is approved for Medicaid, and where I heard it: [PASTE YOUR NOTES] Sort this into three lists: WHAT I WAS TOLD, AND BY WHOM; WHAT I’M ASSUMING; and WHAT I DON’T KNOW. Then turn the second and third lists into questions I could ask a Medicaid planner or the Medicaid agency in my state. Do not answer the questions, and do not fill in rules about notices, renewals, or reporting.

What to look for

How much of the picture is assumption, and a short list of questions in your own words.

What to do next

Keep the questions. You’ll add to them in the next two prompts.

Prompt 2

Find out where the records are

Why this matters

Organized records are the part of this step a family can do years ahead. The hard part is usually not the paperwork itself. It’s that only one person knows where it is.

What you'll need

A rough idea of where your father keeps statements, legal papers, insurance, and care records, and who else can get to them.

Copy this prompt

Here is what I know about where my father’s records are kept and who can get to them: [PASTE YOUR NOTES] Make a table with four columns: the kind of record, where it is kept, who can get to it, and when it was last updated. Group the rows under FINANCIAL, LEGAL, CARE, and OTHER. Where I haven’t said, write “don’t know” instead of guessing. Then list the kinds of records I haven’t mentioned at all, as questions for me to answer. Do not tell me which records Medicaid would require.

What to look for

The “don’t know” cells, and records only one person can reach.

What to do next

Ask your father, or whoever handles his paperwork, to help fill in the blanks.

Prompt 3

Name the changes that may be coming

Why this matters

A move, a sale, a marriage, an inheritance: changes like these are ordinary, and they are also the ones worth asking a professional about before anyone acts.

What you'll need

Anything you expect to change in the next few years. Guesses are fine.

Copy this prompt

I’m planning ahead for my father. Here are the changes our family thinks may be coming over the next few years: [PASTE YOUR NOTES] Group them under INCOME, SAVINGS AND PROPERTY, WHERE HE LIVES, CARE, FAMILY, and MONEY HE MIGHT RECEIVE. For each one, write a question we could ask a professional before acting, and say which kind of professional it likely belongs to: a Medicaid planner, an elder law attorney, a licensed financial professional, or not sure. Do not say how any change would affect Medicaid, and do not suggest what we should do about it.

What to look for

A list of questions, each attached to a real event, with a name for who to ask.

What to do next

Add these to the questions from the first prompt.

Prompt 4

Set a simple review routine

Why this matters

Planning ahead doesn’t mean watching everything all the time. It means agreeing when you’ll look again, and which events would bring the family back to the table sooner.

What you'll need

The results of the first three prompts.

Copy this prompt

Here is what I’ve put together so far: [PASTE THE RESULTS OF PROMPTS 1 TO 3] Write one page with four headings: WHERE OUR RECORDS ARE, WHO WOULD HANDLE WHAT, CHANGES WE’D ASK ABOUT FIRST, and WHEN WE’LL REVIEW. Under the second heading, use only the people I’ve named, and leave a blank line where no one is named. Under the last heading, list the events from my notes that should prompt an earlier look, and leave the review date for me to fill in. Do not say how often Medicaid reviews eligibility, and do not predict whether my father will need it.

What to look for

A page with visible blanks: a record nobody can find, a job nobody has.

What to do next

Share the page with one other family member, agree on a date to look at it again, and bring your question list to the next step below.
